objective: Learners build and use a checklist to inspect at least four real minor-maintenance points around the household, such as a smoke detector's test button, an air or vacuum filter's condition, a cabinet hinge, or a faucet, and report their findings to the household without attempting any repair.
scenario: The learner chooses four or five real check points in the household that commonly need periodic attention, writes what a normal condition versus a needs-attention condition looks like for each one, physically checks each point, and reports the findings to the household so an adult can decide what happens next.
safetyNotes: Checking whether a smoke detector's test button works, a filter looks clean, or a faucet drips is different from repairing any of them; any actual repair, part replacement, or fix beyond a simple check is for the adults in your household, not the learner.

simulationAlternative.description: If the learner cannot safely or physically access certain areas of the household, the learner instead reviews a provided written description of five common minor-maintenance items, decides for each one whether the described condition is normal, needs attention, or needs a trusted adult right away, and drafts the report they would give the household based on those descriptions.

materials: paper or a notes app for the checklist
a flashlight, if needed to see a check point clearly
access to the household areas being checked

tasks.directions: Pick four or five real check points in the household that commonly need periodic attention.

prompts.text: List the check points you picked and name one of them you have never actually looked at closely before.

tasks.directions: For each check point, write what a normal condition looks like and what a needs-attention condition looks like, so you know what you are checking for before you start.

prompts.text: I wrote a normal-condition description and a needs-attention description for at least four check points.
At least one of my check points involves testing something, like pressing a smoke detector's test button, rather than only looking at it.

tasks.directions: Physically check each point on your list against the normal and needs-attention descriptions you wrote, record the actual condition you find for each one, and flag any point that needs a trusted adult's attention.

prompts.text: For each check point, record whether it matched the normal description or the needs-attention description, and describe specifically what you observed.
I did not attempt to fix or repair anything myself, even for a point that needed attention.

tasks.directions: Report your findings to the household.

prompts.text: Describe how you reported your findings to the household, what the household's response was, and name the one check point you think most needs a trusted adult's attention soon.

remediation: If a learner cannot describe what 'normal' looks like for a check point, reteach by having them examine one working example closely first, such as a detector that is known to work or a clean filter, and write the description from that direct comparison before checking the point in question.
extension: Have the learner add two more check points to their list, look into what a trusted household resource, such as an appliance manual or manufacturer's guidance, says about how often each item should be checked, and note that schedule next to each item.
